egin{example} \end{example}[Normalized gradient curve on a square] Source: chow-et-al-ricci-flow-part-iii:page-0465, chow-et-al-ricci-flow-part-iii:page-0521 ↗ ex:chow-iii-h44-square-integral-curves 1. appJ:H.44\group Integral curves

Let $C=[-1,1]^2$ and $f(x,y)=d((x,y),\partial C)$. The maximal integral curve of $ abla f/| abla f|^2$ from $(x,y)$ first runs parallel to a coordinate axis to the nearer diagonal $y=x$ or $y=-x$, and then follows that diagonal to the origin. \end{example}
Proof

\sketch Since $f(x,y)=1-\max \{ |x|,|y|\} $, in each region $|x|>|y|$ or $|y|>|x|$ the gradient points parallel to the coordinate axis which decreases the larger absolute coordinate. The normalized-gradient curve consequently reaches the closest of the two diagonals without changing the smaller absolute coordinate. On a diagonal the generalized gradient is the equal-weight combination of the two adjacent coordinate gradients; its normalized integral curve stays on the diagonal and moves toward the origin. The origin is the maximum set of $f$, so this curve is maximal.
